FOREWORD This Indian Standard ( First Revision) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized by the Environmental Protection Sectional Committee had been approved by the Chemical Division Council. Copper is found mainly as a sulphide, oxide or carbonate in the minerals. Copper enters the water system through mineral dissolution, industrial effluents, because of its use as algicide and insecticide and through corrosion of copper alloy water distribution pipes. It may occur in simple ionic form or in one of many complexes with groups, such as cyanides, chlorides, ammonia or organic ligands. The test for copper is essential because dissolved copper salts even in low concentrations are poisonous to some biota. Desirable limit for copper in potable water is 0�05 mgll maximum which can be relaxed in the absence of better alternate source to 1�5 rna/I. In the preparation of this standard, considerable assistance has been derived from American Society for Testing and Materials, USA ( ASTM Annual Book Section 11, 1983). In reporting th results of a test or analysis made in accordance with this standard, if the final value, observed or calculated, is to be rounded off, it shall be done in accordance with IS 2: 1960 'Rules for rounding off numerical values (revised )9.

1 SCOPE 1.1 This standard prescribes four methods for determination of copper as follows: a) Neocuproine method, b) Atomic absorption method ( direct ), c) Atomic absorption method ( chelation extraction ), and d) Difrerential pulse anodic stripping voltammetry. 1.2 The choice the method depends upon the concentration range and interference. When the concentration levels are below SOO ./1, pre-concentration is carried out either by chelation and extraction prior to atomic abiorptioD spectrophotometer (AAS) or by depolltina as in differential pulse anodic Itrippins voltammetry method. For dissolved copper content filteration through 0�45 lim membrane ftl~er is required. 2 UFERENCES 2.1 The followin, Indian Standards are the necessary adjuncts to this standard: with dilute nitric acid ( 6 N ) prior to the final rinsing with water. The water samples should be collected and stored for 24 h preferably in polypropylene or chemically resistant 81asl containers. For preservation, the samples should be acidified with concentrated nitric acid (2 ml of AR grade nitric acid to 1 litre just to brlng down the pH below 2). Unacidifled samples should be analysed on the same day while the acidified samples may be stored for a few days in a refrigerator. .- QUALITY OF REAGENTS 4.1 Unless specified otherwise, pure chemicals shall be used.

6.2 Interferences
Cadmium, lead, nickel, 'line, cobalt, manganese and chromium up to 10 mg/l do not interfere. Alkali and alkaline earth metals can be tolerated up to 5 000 mg. Iron does not interfere upto 1 000 mg/l.

Adjust the pH by adding sodium hydroxide solution till a blue colour persists. Add dilute hydrochloric acid ( 1 : SO) drop by drop until the colour just disappears. Then add 2�5 ml of dilute hydrocbloric acid to briDI the pH to 2�3 to 2-5. Add 10 ml of pyrrolidinc ditbiocarbamic acid-MIBK realent and shake well. 8.1 Scope ud ApplicatioD
Copper is deposited on a hanging mercury drop at a negative potential of -0�4 V versus saturated calomel electrode. Then the copper is stripped back into the solution by applying a positive potential scan. The anodic current peak which is measured represents the copper concentration in the sample. For total dissolved copper the sample is filtered through � Whatman No.�4O filter paper prior to acidification analysis. This method is applicable in the concentration ranle of 0�1 - 100 1Jt,/1 of copper. 8.2 laterfereaeel Iron interferes when present at levels greater than the copper. This can be overcome by subtracting the anodic peak current for a voltammoffam without deposition from that Cor the atrlppins vcltammcgram. The presence any neighbouring stripping peaks which is les. tban 100 mV from tbat of copper will

interfere.

Same

concentrated nitric acid and rinsing them thorou,hly with distilled water. It the total dissolved copper aJone is to be determined, the sample should be filtered through Whatman No. 40 filter paper. For total recoverable copper, digest the sample with 3 ml each of concentrated hydrocloric acid and nitric acid. Evaporate the solution to 15 to 20 mI. Cool and make up to 100 ml in a volumetric ftask. Tate 10 ml of the sample in the polarographic cell and de-aerate for IS minutes. The cell should be covered with nitrogen gas durin, the experiment (Fi�. 2 ). Generate a new droplet of mercury and put the stirrer on. Connect the cell and deposit at -0�40 V versus saturated calomel electrode for 3 minutes, Stop the stirrer and wait for 30 seconds. Start the. anodic scan with the followins aettings: Initial potential : - 0-4 V vs saturated calomel electrode (SLE) Scan rate : 5 mV/s Scan direction : + Modulation amplitude: 25 mV Current range : 1 - 10 ,.,.A Droptime : S sec Display direction : <:: Low pass filter : Off position Mode : Differential pulse Scan range : 0�75 V Measuse the current peak height (11). Add 20 "I of standard copper (II) solution and de-aerate for 5 minutes. Repeat as above. Measure the current peak height ( 1. ).
